takeaways: Case 4 (QBL) was the gift case: a 6-mark GST valuation that is one division (₹8,85,000 ÷ 1.18), plus 9 marks of pure theory. Spend the first 15 minutes finding such questions before you choose your four cases.

Most descriptive marks were ready-made lists in the SM: Ind AS 1 para 117B, AFM currency-risk parameters, s.230(7) proviso, Clause (1) Part I Second Schedule, the VFM Es. Know which chapter holds which list and you write straight from the book.
Small words decided answers: 'non-cumulative', 'Pvt. Ltd.' vs 'partnership firm', '₹5,000 a day', 'put to use 15 Oct', 'more than one WTD', 'dormant'. Underline them on the first read.

Seven keys in this paper are debatable or defective (1.1, 1.4, 1.5, 2.7, 3.2, 3.4, 5.2). When no option fits cleanly, pick the closest and write one line of reasoning. The examiner reads your answer book, so the reasoning can earn the marks.
Corporate law came as much from SEBI LODR as from the Companies Act (Reg 17A seven listed boards, Reg 24 10%/20% tests, Reg 23 subsidiary RPTs). Keep these thresholds on one page.

cases.title: Renewable Energy Systems Limited (RESL)
cases.industry: Renewable energy components: manufacture, export and solar maintenance
cases.story: A listed Noida company that makes and exports renewable-energy components. It wants two more directors, plans to fund the takeover of supplier TCL with OCPS, and has two GST problems: a rate change and a show cause notice after a short payment.
cases.first15: Pick it if GST is your strength: 8 marks are IDT (rate change, bill-to-ship-to, s.74A), and 1.7 (4 marks for one proviso) plus 1.8 (Gordon/Walter) are quick. Beware: 3 of its 5 MCQs (1.1, 1.4, 1.5) have debatable keys.

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Corporate Laws (SPOM Set A): Appointment and Qualifications of Directors
questions.topic: More than 15 directors: s.149(1) proviso; altering articles u/s 14
questions.ask: The board has 14 directors, the Articles allow 15, and two more are to be added (16 in all). Which listed compliance steps are NOT correct?
questions.clue: "BoD of RESL comprises 14 Directors... Articles... permit a maximum strength of 15"
think: 14 + Mr P + Mr Q = 16, which is above both the Articles' cap and the Act's cap of 15. So the question is about the s.149(1) ceiling.
Chapter clear -> Corporate Laws -> Appointment of directors -> s.149(1) proviso: more than 15 only after a special resolution.
The Articles also fix 15, so they must be altered. Under s.14 that needs a special resolution, never an ordinary one. The 2013 Act has no ROC or Central Government approval for this.
(i) and (iv) are surely wrong, so only (C) or (D) can be right. ICAI treats (iii) 'pass a special resolution' as the one correct step.

look_up.where: ICAI SM Corporate & Economic Laws: Appointment and Qualifications of Directors

questions.solve:
S.149(1): a public company may have up to 15 directors, and more than 15 only after passing a special resolution. RESL's Articles also cap the board at 15, so the Articles must be altered, and s.14 requires a special resolution for that.
(i) Alter Articles by ordinary resolution: wrong.
(iv) Ordinary resolution + ROC approval: wrong. There is no Government/ROC approval under the 2013 Act; that was the 1956 Act route.
(iii) Pass a special resolution: right.
(ii) Alter Articles and pass a special resolution: this also describes the legally complete route, but ICAI marks it 'not correct' because one special resolution in general meeting can alter the Articles and approve the higher number together.
questions.answer: (C) (i), (ii) and (iv)
questions.flag: Debatable: (ii) is also a valid step (alter the Articles' cap of 15 by special resolution, plus a special resolution u/s 149(1)). Strictly only (i) and (iv) are wrong, and no option gives that set. ICAI picked (C).
questions.trap: Choosing an ordinary resolution or ROC/Central Government approval. That was the 1956 Act route.

questions.subject: Audit
questions.chapter: Quality Control (SQC 1 and SA 220)
questions.topic: Engagement quality control reviewer: objectivity; consultation by the engagement partner
questions.ask: Which actions can the EQCR, CA. S, take without compromising his objectivity?
questions.clue: "CA. H decided to consult the Engagement Quality Control Reviewer, CA. S"
think: EQCR + 'objectivity' -> SQC 1 / SA 220. The EQCR reviews the work but never takes part in it or decides for the team.
Chapter clear -> Audit SM -> Quality Control -> 'objectivity of the engagement quality control reviewer' and 'EQC review for listed entities'.
Allowed: reviewing significant judgements (materiality), being consulted by the partner, reviewing the consultations. Not allowed: making decisions for the team. Strike (iii) -> (C).

look_up.where: ICAI SM Audit: Quality Control (SQC 1 / SA 220)

questions.solve:
For a listed entity, the EQC review covers the team's significant judgements (especially materiality and significant risks), whether proper consultation took place on contentious matters and what was concluded, and the proposed report. The engagement partner may consult the reviewer during the audit, and that alone does not impair objectivity. To stay objective, the reviewer must not otherwise take part in the engagement or make decisions for the team.
(i) Allowed (reviewing materiality judgements). (ii) Allowed (being consulted on conclusions). (iv) Allowed (reviewing consultations). (iii) Not allowed.
questions.answer: (C) (i), (ii) and (iv)
questions.trap: Treating any consultation with the engagement partner as a breach. Consultation is allowed; making decisions for the team is not.

questions.subject: AFM
questions.chapter: Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
questions.topic: Strategic financial management: capital as the limiting factor in resource allocation
questions.ask: Under the strategic financial management approach, which items are NOT limiting factors when allocating resources?
questions.clue: "strategically allocating scarce capital resources among competing opportunities"
think: 'Approach suggested by management' = Strategic Financial Management. It is not obvious which chapter covers that, so use the A-Z index -> 'strategic financial management' -> AFM Chapter 1.
AFM -> Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy -> 'strategic financial decision making framework'.
The SM says capital is the limiting factor, so management must spread limited funds across alternative uses. Only capital availability is a constraint.
Mode of financing, the best opportunities and future earnings are things you choose between, not constraints -> (A).

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM: Ch 1 Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

questions.solve: The AFM SM says capital is the limiting factor. The strategic problem is to allocate limited funds among alternative uses so that investor returns are kept up or increased. So (ii) capital availability is the limiting factor. (i) mode of financing, (iii) best investment opportunities and (iv) future earnings potential are decision variables, not limits.
questions.answer: (A) (i), (iii) and (iv)
questions.trap: Treating 'mode of financing' as a constraint because RESL is raising OCPS. It is a choice, not the limit.

questions.subject: FR
questions.chapter: Ind AS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation
questions.topic: Compound financial instrument: splitting an OCPS into liability and equity
questions.ask: What is the equity component per OCPS on initial recognition? Terms: face value ₹100, 5% non-cumulative dividend, convertible into 5 shares, redeemable after 8 years, market rate 8%.
questions.clue: "Optionally Convertible Preference Shares... convertible into 5 equity shares, redeemable after 8 years"
think: Convertible + redeemable + 'equity component' = a compound instrument -> Ind AS 32 split.
Chapter clear -> FR -> Ind AS 32 -> the 'compound financial instruments' illustration. Copy its method and change the figures.
Value the liability first: PV of contractual cash flows at 8% (the rate for a non-convertible instrument). Equity is the residual.
The options assume the dividend is contractual: PV of dividends 28.73 + PV of redemption 54.03 = 82.76 -> equity 17.24.

look_up.where: ICAI SM FR: Ind AS 32 Financial Instruments: Presentation

questions.solve:
Residual method (Ind AS 32 para 31-32): measure the liability at the PV of contractual cash flows at 8%; equity = proceeds − liability.
PV of dividends: ₹5 × 5.7466 = ₹28.73
PV of redemption: ₹100 × 0.5403 = ₹54.03
Liability = ₹82.76
Equity = ₹100 − ₹82.76 = ₹17.24 (ICAI key)
Strict view: a non-cumulative dividend paid at RESL's discretion is not a contractual obligation. Under Ind AS 32 AG37 the liability is only the PV of redemption (₹54.03) and equity is ₹45.97, which is not among the options. The conversion option being out of the money does not change the split; the residual still goes to equity.
questions.answer: (B) ₹17.24 per OCPS. It is the only option produced by the residual method. A strict Ind AS 32 reading gives ₹45.97, which is not offered.
questions.flag: ICAI treats the 5% non-cumulative (discretionary) dividend as a liability. Under Ind AS 32 AG37 it is equity, so equity = ₹100 − ₹54.03 = ₹45.97, which is not an option.
questions.trap: Picking ₹82.76 (that is the liability) or ₹54.03 (the PV of principal). The question asks for the equity component.

questions.subject: IDT
questions.chapter: Time of Supply (s.14 CGST); Place of Supply (s.10 IGST)
questions.topic: Change in rate of tax; goods ordered by an unregistered buyer and delivered to a third person
questions.ask: Is 18% the right GST rate on the ABC service? What is the place of supply for goods ordered by FG (Rohtak) but delivered to VC (Jalandhar)?

options.a: Correct GST rate: 18%. Place of Supply is Rohtak
options.b: Correct GST rate: 12%. Place of Supply is Jalandhar
options.c: Correct GST rate: 12%. Place of Supply is Rohtak
options.d: Correct GST rate: 18%. Place of Supply is Jalandhar

questions.clue: "changed from 12% to 18% with effect from 21/07/2025"; "recorded delivery address of Jalandhar"
think: Two parts. The rate changed mid-transaction -> s.14 'change in rate of tax'. Ordered by one person, shipped to another -> place of supply, s.10(1) IGST.
Chapter clear -> IDT -> Time of Supply -> s.14 table. Service done before the change, payment before, invoice after -> date of payment -> old rate 12%.
Place of supply: FG is unregistered. ICAI applies s.10(1)(ca) (unregistered buyer -> address recorded in the invoice) and takes Jalandhar.
Only (B) has 12% + Jalandhar.

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT: Time of Supply; Place of Supply
index_keywords: change in rate of tax section 14
supply to unregistered person address recorded in invoice

questions.solve:
Rate:
• Service completed 20/07, before the change.
• Payment received 15/07, before the change.
• Invoice issued 22/07, after the change.
S.14(a)(iii): if supply is before the change, the invoice after and the payment before, time of supply = date of payment (15/07). So the old rate of 12% applies, and charging 18% is wrong.
Place of supply: FG Industries is unregistered, and the invoice records the delivery address in Jalandhar. ICAI applies s.10(1)(ca): for goods supplied to an unregistered person, place of supply = location as per the address recorded in the invoice. That gives Jalandhar (Punjab), so IGST applies, not Haryana tax.
Alternative view: under the bill-to-ship-to rule in s.10(1)(b), FG (which directed the delivery) is deemed the recipient. Place of supply is then its principal place of business, Rohtak.
questions.answer: (B) Correct GST rate 12%; place of supply Jalandhar
questions.flag: Debatable: on bill-to-ship-to facts, s.10(1)(b) deems FG (which directed the delivery) the recipient, giving Rohtak (option C). ICAI instead applies the unregistered-buyer rule u/s 10(1)(ca) and reads the invoice's delivery address.
questions.trap: Taking 18% because the invoice was raised after the change. When payment came first, the payment date fixes the rate.

questions.subject: IDT
questions.chapter: Demands and Recovery (s.74A / s.74 CGST)
questions.topic: Fraud/suppression demand: payment before SCN with 15% penalty, shortfall, 25%/50% options
questions.ask: Can the department issue an SCN after RESL paid tax, interest and penalty? Did RESL pay the right penalty? What remedy does RESL have? (2 + 4 marks)
questions.clue: "misrepresentation of facts and proper officer before serving show cause notice"
think: 'Misrepresentation' + 'before SCN' + penalty paid -> a fraud/suppression demand: s.74A (FY 2024-25 onwards); old s.74 for earlier years.
Chapter clear -> IDT -> Demands and Recovery -> s.74A ladder: 15% before SCN, 25% within 60 days of SCN, 50% within 60 days of order.
Compare: tax ascertained ₹10 lakh vs paid ₹8 lakh; penalty due 15% × ₹8 lakh = ₹1.20 lakh vs paid ₹0.80 lakh.
Conclude: no SCN for the amount fully paid; SCN is valid for the shortfall. Remedy: pay with a 25% or 50% penalty and close the case, or contest it.

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT: Demands and Recovery
index_keywords: fraud wilful misstatement suppression of facts

questions.solve:
Provision (fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression; s.74A for FY 2024-25 onwards): before an SCN, the person may pay the tax, s.50 interest and a penalty of 15% of that tax, on his own ascertainment or the officer's, and inform the officer. No SCN is then served for the tax so paid. If the officer finds the payment short, he issues an SCN for the shortfall.
Facts: tax communicated ₹10,00,000; paid ₹8,00,000.
Penalty required = 15% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. Paid ₹80,000 (10%), so ₹40,000 short. If the ₹80,000 covered interest as well, the shortfall is larger.
So there can be no SCN for the ₹8 lakh, but an SCN can be issued for the balance tax of ₹2,00,000 with interest and penalty, plus the penalty shortfall. Management's view is wrong.
questions.answer:
Part 1 (2 marks)
• Provision: in fraud/suppression cases (s.74A), if tax + interest + a 15% penalty are paid before the SCN, no SCN is issued for the tax so paid. If the payment is short, an SCN is issued for the shortfall.
• Analysis: tax ascertained ₹10 lakh, paid ₹8 lakh. Penalty due = 15% of ₹8 lakh = ₹1,20,000; paid ₹80,000 (10%), so ₹40,000 short.
• Conclusion: no SCN can be issued for the ₹8 lakh already covered. An SCN can be issued for the unpaid tax of ₹2 lakh with interest and penalty, and for the ₹40,000 penalty shortfall. RESL has NOT deposited the required penalty.

Part 2 (4 marks): Remedies available to RESL
1. Within 60 days of the SCN: pay tax + interest + a penalty of 25% of the tax. All proceedings on that notice are then deemed concluded.
2. Within 60 days of communication of the order: pay tax + interest + a penalty of 50% of the tax. All proceedings are then deemed concluded.
3. If it disputes the demand: reply to the SCN. Against the order, appeal u/s 107 within 3 months after a pre-deposit of 10% of the disputed tax.
(For periods up to FY 2023-24, the same 15%/25%/50% scheme applies under s.74, with 30-day windows.)
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI: SCN for ₹2 lakh + interest + penalty, penalty short by ₹40,000, and the 25%/50% options within 60 days. The appeal route is an extra point.
questions.trap: Saying no SCN can be issued at all because 'tax was paid'. The protection covers only the amount paid with the full 15% penalty.

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations (Companies Act, 2013)
questions.topic: Auditor's certificate on accounting treatment: provisos to s.230(7) and s.232(3)
questions.ask: If the TCL acquisition goes through an NCLT scheme of arrangement, what certificate is needed from RESL's statutory auditor?
questions.clue: "structured as a Scheme of Arrangement involving the NCLT... certification... from the Statutory Auditor"
think: 'Scheme of arrangement' + 'NCLT' + 'auditor certificate' -> s.230/232 of the Companies Act.
Chapter clear -> Law -> Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations -> s.230(7) proviso (and the s.232(3) proviso for mergers).

You know this one: write it without the book. The certificate says the scheme's accounting treatment conforms to the accounting standards u/s 133. For 4 marks, add who gives it, its content, the listed-company angle and a conclusion.

look_up.where: ICAI SM Corporate & Economic Laws: Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations

questions.solve: Proviso to s.230(7): NCLT shall not sanction a compromise or arrangement unless the company's auditor has filed a certificate that the accounting treatment, if any, proposed in the scheme conforms to the accounting standards prescribed u/s 133. The proviso to s.232(3) says the same for merger/amalgamation schemes. The scheme is RESL's, so its statutory auditors give the certificate. Being listed, RESL also files this auditor's certificate with the stock exchange along with the draft scheme (SEBI scheme framework).
questions.answer:
• Provision: proviso to s.230(7) [s.232(3) for a merger/amalgamation]. NCLT will not sanction a scheme unless the company's auditor certifies that the accounting treatment proposed in it conforms to the accounting standards notified u/s 133 (Ind AS for RESL).
• Who: RESL's statutory auditors, M/s HK & Associates, file the certificate with the Tribunal.
• Content: the accounting proposed in the scheme for the TCL acquisition (e.g., Ind AS 103 business combination) complies with Ind AS. Any deviation must be removed before sanction.
• Listed company: the same auditor's certificate also goes to the stock exchange with the draft scheme under SEBI's framework for schemes.
• Conclusion: NCLT must obtain the auditor's certificate that the scheme's accounting treatment conforms to the accounting standards before it sanctions the scheme.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI. The s.232(3) and SEBI points are extra.
questions.trap: Writing about a valuation report or fairness opinion. Those come from a registered valuer or merchant banker, not from the auditor.

questions.subject: AFM
questions.chapter: Security Valuation (Dividend Discount Model); Dividend Decisions (Walter's model)
questions.topic: Share price from book value and ROE: Gordon growth model and Walter's model
questions.ask: With Ke of 15%, value TCL's share using (a) the Dividend Growth Model and (b) Walter's model.
questions.clue: "TCL's current book value is ₹400 per share, Return on equity is 12%"
think: The question names both models, so this is a pure numerical. TCL follows the 'same policy' as RESL, so retention is 70% and payout 30%.
Build the inputs: EPS = BV × ROE; DPS = 30% of EPS; g = b × r.
Chapter clear -> AFM Security Valuation (Gordon) / Inter FM Dividend Decisions (Walter). You know the formulae; solve without the book.
Add the D0-vs-D1 alternative in one line. ICAI accepts both.

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM: Security Valuation; Inter FM: Dividend Decisions

questions.answer:
Working notes: EPS = ₹400 × 12% = ₹48; payout 30% -> DPS ₹14.40; retention 70% -> g = 0.70 × 12% = 8.4%; Ke = 15%.

(a) Dividend Growth (Gordon) Model
P0 = D1 ÷ (Ke − g) = 14.40 ÷ (0.15 − 0.084) = 14.40 ÷ 0.066 = ₹218.18
(Alternative, treating ₹14.40 as D0: D1 = ₹15.61 -> P0 = ₹236.52)

(b) Walter's Model
P = [D + (r/Ke)(E − D)] ÷ Ke
= [14.40 + (0.12/0.15)(48.00 − 14.40)] ÷ 0.15
= (14.40 + 26.88) ÷ 0.15 = ₹275.20
(Alternative with growth-adjusted E ₹52.03 and D ₹15.61: ₹298.33)

Comment: r (12%) is below Ke (15%), so retaining 70% lowers value. On Walter's logic, a 100% payout would give 48 ÷ 0.15 = ₹320.
questions.icai: Same as ICAI: ₹218.18 (alt ₹236.52) and ₹275.20 (alt ₹298.33). The payout comment is extra.
questions.trap: Using ROE (12%) as the growth rate, or swapping retention and payout. g = retention ratio × ROE = 8.4%.

cases.title: XYZ Metal Industries Limited (XYZ)
cases.industry: Stainless steel pipes and fittings manufacturing
cases.story: A listed steel-pipe maker with a listed subsidiary (JBS) and a 45% stake in PQR. Sales and profit are falling because of quality failures and old machines. It is importing CNC machines with £ debt, swapping ESOPs with JBS, and facing a limit-on-directorships question.
cases.first15: Skip candidate: 2.2 (Ind AS 110 potential voting rights) and 2.7 (group ESOP cancellation, with no figure for year 2) are tough. The 6-mark cost-of-quality report is the only easy block, and the marks printed in the SA add up to only 24.

questions.subject: Costing
questions.chapter: SCPM: Lean System and Innovation
questions.topic: Lean tools: standardised work, JIT, visual management, value stream mapping
questions.ask: Which rows of Mr Rajiv's issue -> corrective-measure matrix are correctly matched?
questions.clue: "recommended the adoption of lean manufacturing practices"
think: Standardised work, JIT, visual management and value stream are all lean tools -> SCPM Lean chapter.
Chapter clear -> SCPM -> Lean System and Innovation -> read the one-line purpose of each tool.
(a) uniform procedures = standardised work ✓. (c) search-free, count-free = visual management ✓. (d) see every step, remove non-value-added work = value stream ✓.
(b): JIT removes WASTE (over-production) by producing only what is needed. 'Eliminating all defects at source' is jidoka/zero defects, so the match is wrong -> (B).

look_up.where: ICAI SM SCPM: Lean System and Innovation

questions.solve:
(a) Standardised work: one documented best method that cuts variability and eases training. Match.
(b) JIT: produce only what is needed, when it is needed, to cut waste (over-production, inventory). 'Eliminating all defects / quality at source' describes jidoka or zero-defect tools, not JIT. Mismatch.
(c) Visual management: items placed and labelled so they can be found and counted at a glance. Match.
(d) Value stream (mapping): shows every step of the flow and exposes non-value-added activities. Match.
questions.answer: (B) (a), (c) and (d)
questions.trap: Accepting (b) because 'producing only as needed' is JIT's definition. The catch is that 'waste' has been swapped for 'defects'.

questions.subject: FR
questions.chapter: Ind AS 110 Consolidated Financial Statements
questions.topic: Control through a forward contract: potential voting rights giving present access to returns; NCI split; Ind AS 109 scope
questions.ask: XYZ holds 45% of PQR. On 01.07.2025 it enters a forward to buy 12% more. Which statements on control, the NCI split and the forward's accounting are right?
questions.clue: "entitled to receive any dividends... exercise its voting rights... instructions of XYZ"
think: 45% + a contract giving XYZ the votes and dividends on another 12% -> is that control? -> Ind AS 110 (power, returns, link).
Chapter clear -> FR -> Ind AS 110 -> Appendix B 'potential voting rights' and 'present ownership interest' (B89-B91).
Votes: 45% + 12% directed by XYZ = 57% -> power. Dividends on the 12% -> present access to returns -> allocate 57% / 43%.
B91: such instruments fall outside Ind AS 109 -> (iv) true, (iii) false -> (D).

look_up.where: ICAI SM FR: Ind AS 110 Consolidated Financial Statements

questions.solve:
Power: XYZ holds 45%, and from 01.07.2025 B Ltd must vote its 12% as XYZ instructs. XYZ therefore directs 57% of the votes; the other 43% sits with A (19%) and C (18%). XYZ controls PQR from 01.07.2025, so (i) is true.
Returns: XYZ receives the dividends on the 12% now, so in substance it already has an ownership interest. Under B90, profit/OCI is allocated 57% to the parent and 43% to NCI, so (ii) is true.
B91: when potential voting rights already give access to the returns of a consolidated subsidiary, the instrument is not accounted for under Ind AS 109. So (iii) is false and (iv) is true.
questions.answer: (D) (i), (ii) and (iv)
questions.trap: Treating the forward as a derivative at FVTPL under Ind AS 109. It is absorbed into consolidation.

questions.subject: AFM
questions.chapter: Interest Rate Risk Management (swaps); Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
questions.topic: Comparative advantage in borrowing; forwards vs currency futures
questions.ask: Which statements on the £ borrowing choice and on XYZ's forward / JBS's futures are correct?
questions.clue: "fixed rate of 5.5% or... 60 basis points above SONIA"
think: Two firms with fixed and floating quotes -> comparative advantage / interest rate swap logic.
Chapter clear -> AFM -> Interest Rate Risk Management (swaps) + Forex chapter (forward vs futures).
Fixed gap 6.5 − 5.5 = 1.00%; floating gap 1.15 − 0.60 = 0.55%. XYZ's edge is bigger in fixed, so XYZ borrows fixed, JBS borrows floating, and they swap.
Forward = OTC, priced through the bid-ask spread, no MTM. Futures = exchange-traded, brokerage, daily MTM -> (i) and (iii).

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM: Interest Rate Risk Management; Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

questions.solve:
Quotes: XYZ fixed 5.5% or SONIA + 0.60; JBS fixed 6.5% or SONIA + 1.15.
XYZ's advantage is 1.00% in fixed and 0.55% in floating, so it is larger in fixed. XYZ borrows fixed, JBS borrows floating, and they swap; the 0.45% total gain is shared. XYZ ends up paying floating, which it wants because it expects rates to fall. (i) true.
(ii) False: currency futures trade on an exchange; only the forward is OTC.
(iii) True: a forward's cost is built into the bank's bid-ask spread; futures carry brokerage.
(iv) False: forwards are not marked to market; futures are. Ignore the stray line that JBS's contract is not settled daily; the options are built on the standard features.
questions.answer: (B) (i) and (iii)
questions.trap: Putting XYZ on floating because XYZ wants floating. First borrow where you have the comparative edge, then swap.

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Appointment and Qualifications of Directors (s.165); SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015
questions.topic: Limits on directorships: s.165 (20 total / 10 public) and Reg 17A (7 listed entities)
questions.ask: Is Mr Suresh eligible to join XYZ as a Whole-Time Director, given his existing directorships?

options.a: Eligible: counting private subsidiaries of public companies and excluding inactive companies, his countable directorships are well within the limit.
options.b: Eligible: his listed-company directorships are within the limit and he has not crossed the overall cap across private and public companies.
options.c: Ineligible: private subsidiaries are included and inactive companies excluded, and the overall cap is not crossed, but his directorships in listed companies exceed the SEBI limit.
options.d: Ineligible: he has already exceeded the maximum directorships in publicly traded companies and also the limit for total directorships in listed companies.

questions.clue: "one dormant company, eight Public Limited companies, of which seven are listed"
think: Counting directorships -> s.165 (20 total, 10 public). XYZ is listed, so SEBI LODR Reg 17A (7 listed) applies too.
Chapter clear -> Law -> Appointment of directors -> s.165 explanations (dormant excluded; a private subsidiary of a public company counts as public). SEBI LODR -> Reg 17A.
Count after joining XYZ: total 19 + 1 = 20 ✓; public 8 + 1 (JBS's private subsidiary) + 1 = 10 ✓; listed 7 + 1 = 8 ✗ (max 7).
He fails only the SEBI listed-entity cap -> (C).

look_up.where: ICAI SM Corporate & Economic Laws: Appointment and Qualifications of Directors; SEBI (LODR)
index_keywords: private company subsidiary of public company

questions.solve:
S.165: a maximum of 20 companies (dormant companies excluded), of which at most 10 public. A private company that is a holding or subsidiary of a public company counts as public.
Existing: 1 dormant (ignore); 8 public; 11 private, of which 1 is a subsidiary of JBS (a listed public company) and so counts as public.
Total countable = 8 + 11 = 19; with XYZ = 20, within 20.
Public = 8 + 1 = 9; with XYZ = 10, within 10.
Reg 17A(1) LODR: no person may be a director in more than 7 listed entities. He already sits on 7 listed boards; XYZ is listed and would be the 8th, which exceeds the cap. He is ineligible.
questions.answer: (C) Ineligible. The Companies Act limits (20 total, 10 public) are met, but XYZ would be his 8th listed directorship against SEBI's cap of 7.
questions.trap: Rejecting him under s.165 because he 'holds 20'. The dormant company drops out, so the Companies Act limit is still met.

questions.subject: Audit
questions.chapter: Review of Financial Information (SRE 2410)
questions.topic: Limited review of interim financial information: required procedures
questions.ask: Which procedures must the audit firm perform when reviewing the quarterly interim financial information?
questions.clue: "interim financial information for the quarter ended 31st December 2025"

questions.solve:
Classification (₹ lakh):
Prevention = training and audits 10 + preventive maintenance 20 = 30 (10%)
Appraisal = incoming inspection and equipment testing 18 (6%)
Conformance = 48 (16%)
Internal failure = rework and downtime 117 (39%)
External failure = warranty and complaints 135 (45%)

Total = 300

questions.answer:
REPORT
To: Board of Directors, XYZ Metal Industries Ltd
From: Management Accounting Department
Subject: Analysis of quality costs and measures to reduce quality failures

1. Statement of Cost of Quality (₹ lakh; % of total)
Prevention: quality training and audits 10 (3.33%); preventive maintenance 20 (6.67%). Total 30 (10%)
Appraisal: inspection of incoming materials and equipment testing 18 (6%)
Cost of conformance: 48 (16%)
Internal failure: rework and production downtime 117 (39%)
External failure: warranty claims and customer complaints 135 (45%)
Cost of non-conformance: 252 (84%)
Total cost of quality: 300 (100%)

2. Analysis
• 84% of quality spend goes on failures and only 16% on preventing or detecting them. XYZ fixes defects after they happen.
• External failure (45%) is the largest block: warranty claims, returns and complaints. It also costs orders: turnover fell from ₹850 crore to ₹800 crore and PAT from ₹35 crore to ₹30 crore, while new entrants offer better quality at lower prices.
• Internal failure (39%): rework and downtime come from frequent breakdowns, outdated machines and staff turnover, and they delay customer orders.
• Fittings built to old standards and the stock of discontinued stainless items point to weak design control and poor production-marketing planning.
• Preventive maintenance (₹20 lakh) is small compared with downtime and rework (₹117 lakh).

3. Recommendations
(a) Total Productive Maintenance: planned and autonomous maintenance, machine-wise schedules over each asset's life, and tracking of equipment effectiveness. This targets breakdowns, downtime and rework (internal failure).
(b) Total Quality Management: right first time, employee involvement and training, statistical process control, designs updated to current industry standards, and supplier quality assurance (e.g., third-party inspection at the supplier's site). This targets defects reaching customers (external failure).
(c) Shift spend towards prevention and appraisal: in-process inspection, design reviews and mistake-proofing. Back the planned CNC machines with operator training.
(d) Lean housekeeping: JIT purchasing and 5S to stop the build-up of raw material and obsolete stock.

4. Conclusion
Spending more on conformance will cut the much larger failure cost. The aim is the balance at which the total cost of quality is lowest and customers stop sending goods back.

Management Accountant
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI: 16% conformance vs 84% non-conformance; TPM and TQM recommended.
questions.trap: Putting items in the wrong bucket. Training and audits = prevention; incoming inspection and testing = appraisal (as ICAI classified them).

Chapter clear -> Audit SM -> SRE 2410 -> 'matter that causes the auditor to believe a material adjustment may be needed' and 'modified conclusion'.

questions.solve:
Yes. When a matter makes the auditor believe the interim information may be materially misstated, he makes additional inquiries or performs other procedures (substantive ones if needed) until he can reach a conclusion.
Inventory procedures: ask how management identifies obsolete and slow-moving items and estimates NRV; get the ageing and non-moving lists and compare them with the last year-end; check the write-down working against current selling prices, scrap rates and sales after the quarter; discuss the fittings built to old standards and the discontinued stainless line with the Production and Marketing heads; run analytics on inventory days and gross margin; read board minutes on the discontinuation; obtain a written representation on inventory valuation; inspect physically or confirm if needed.
Reporting: material misstatement -> qualified conclusion ('except for') if not pervasive, adverse if pervasive. Evidence not obtained -> qualified if the possible effect is material but not pervasive, disclaimer if pervasive. Communicate to management and the audit committee.
questions.answer:
• Can he do more? Yes. Under SRE 2410, if a matter suggests the interim financial information may be materially misstated, the auditor makes additional inquiries or performs other procedures so that he can express a conclusion.
• Additional procedures for obsolete and non-moving inventory:
  1. Ask the CFO and the production/stores heads how obsolete and slow-moving items are identified and how NRV is estimated.
  2. Obtain the ageing and non-moving inventory list; check that the outdated fittings and the discontinued stainless-steel stock appear in it.
  3. Recompute the write-down: compare cost with NRV using recent selling prices, scrap values and sales after the quarter.
  4. Analytical procedures: inventory holding days, gross margin, and provision as % of inventory compared with earlier quarters.
  5. Read board/committee minutes on discontinuing the product line.
  6. Where needed, physically inspect the obsolete stock or test details.
  7. Obtain a written representation from management on inventory valuation.
• Reporting:
  (a) Valuation materially misstated: qualified conclusion (material, not pervasive) or adverse conclusion (material and pervasive), with a basis paragraph stating the effect.
  (b) Sufficient appropriate evidence not obtained: qualified conclusion (possible effect material, not pervasive) or disclaimer of conclusion (material and pervasive).
  (c) Communicate the matter to management and the audit committee.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI. ICAI quotes SRE 2400 ('practitioner') wording; a listed company's quarterly limited review by its own auditor falls under SRE 2410, and the reporting outcome is the same.
questions.trap: Saying a review allows no extra procedures. Limited assurance still needs more work when something looks wrong.

VFM evaluation of EHT, FY 2024-25
1. Economy (getting inputs at the lowest cost for the required quality)
• Dustbins at ₹400 against an MRP of ₹700: ₹7.5 lakh saved on 2,500 bins.
• 12,000 trees from ₹5 lakh of saplings (about ₹42 per tree); solar panels at 25% lower installation cost; discounted medical equipment and materials; a modest ₹4.5 lakh a year honorarium per doctor.
• Critique: the ₹75 lakh first-of-its-kind import shows no quotations, tendering or life-cycle costing.
2. Efficiency (output per rupee or per input)
• 2,560 eye surgeries, 22,000+ patients, 60 camps, 50 cleanliness campaigns and 2,500 bins distributed; digital records cut administrative cost.
• Critique: no cost per surgery or patient, equipment utilisation, downtime or patients per doctor is reported, so efficiency is claimed rather than measured.
3. Effectiveness (were the objectives achieved?)
• A government survey shows a visible fall in litter and a rise in vegetation cover; successful surgeries restore vision; preventive programmes target disease incidence.
• Critique: no post-operative outcome or complication data, tree survival rate, or evidence that waste-segregation habits lasted.
4. Equity (fair access for those in need)
• Sliding-scale fees, free treatment for those who cannot pay, outreach in underserved areas, free dustbins.
• Critique: no data on who was served (income group, gender, age, disability, remote villages), so fairness cannot be shown.
Conclusion: EHT scores well on Economy and on outputs. It should set KPIs and targets for outcomes and equity, and report them to donors, to prove value for money. (Ethics can be added as a fifth 'E'.)

questions.subject: AFM
questions.chapter: Risk Management
questions.topic: Types of risk: operational, financial (currency), compliance, strategic
questions.ask: Identify and explain any three risks EHT faces by importing first-of-its-kind equipment for eye surgeries.
questions.clue: "imported latest medical equipment (first of its kind in India) worth ₹75 lakh"
think: 'Identify risks' could be AFM or Strategic Management. Unsure -> A-Z index -> 'types of risk' -> AFM Risk Management (strategic, operational, financial, compliance).
AFM -> Risk Management -> 'identification of types of risk faced by an organisation'.
Match the facts: 'first of its kind' -> operational/technology risk; 'imported' -> currency risk; imported + FCRA funds + medical device -> compliance risk.
4 marks -> 3 risks, each with its meaning, the case link and the effect, plus a short mitigation.

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM: Risk Management

questions.solve:
Pick three and tie each to a case fact:
• Operational/technology: no trained users, no local service, spares abroad, downtime.
• Currency: price, spares and service contracts in foreign currency; rupee depreciation.
• Compliance: FEMA/Customs import rules, a CDSCO licence under the Medical Devices Rules, and, if the purchase used foreign contribution, FCRA rules on use and records (EHT keeps no separate FC records).
questions.answer:
1. Operational (technology) risk: the equipment is the first of its kind in India, so there are no trained surgeons or technicians, no local service engineers and no ready spares. A breakdown means long downtime, fewer surgeries and costly overseas support. Mitigation: vendor training, a comprehensive maintenance contract with a guaranteed response time, and a stock of critical spares.
2. Currency (financial) risk: the price, spares, consumables and software updates are in foreign currency. A falling rupee raises the cost of any unpaid amount and of future upkeep, squeezing a trust that runs on fixed donations. Mitigation: forward cover on payables and rupee-priced maintenance contracts.
3. Compliance (regulatory) risk: the import must follow FEMA/Customs rules and medical-device import licensing (CDSCO). If paid from foreign contribution, it must be paid from the FCRA utilisation account and recorded separately, and EHT keeps no separate FC records. A breach can bring penalties or suspension of FCRA registration. Mitigation: a compliance checklist and a separate FC asset register.
(Also acceptable: strategic or obsolescence risk, since unproven technology may not deliver the expected outcomes.)
questions.icai: Same as ICAI: operational, currency and compliance risks.
questions.trap: Listing risks with no link to 'first of its kind' or 'imported'. The marks come from the case link.

questions.subject: Costing
questions.chapter: SCPM: Introduction to Strategic Cost Management (Value Chain Analysis); TQM
questions.topic: Porter's value chain primary activities: making the spice blends in-house instead of buying them
questions.ask: In a TQM setting, analyse how making the spice blends in-house (Division-A) instead of buying them from outside vendors affects each primary activity in QBL's value chain.
questions.clue: "primary activities of QBL's Value Chain"; "source high-grade spice blends internally"
think: 'Primary activities' + 'value chain' -> Porter: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service.
Chapter clear -> SCPM -> Value chain analysis (also in Strategic Management, internal environment). You know it; write without the book.
For each activity: the gain, the cost, the TQM link and a case fact (Agra kitchen, Division-D and G demand, Germany).
6 marks -> 5 activities × 2-3 lines + a conclusion.

look_up.where: ICAI SM SCPM: Introduction to Strategic Cost Management (Value Chain Analysis)

questions.solve: Take each primary activity in turn: state the net effect and the TQM angle, then give an overall view.
questions.answer:
Impact of in-house spice blends on QBL's primary activities (TQM lens)
1. Inbound logistics: QBL now buys raw spices, not finished blends. It controls purity, hygiene, traceability and supply timing, with less vendor quality risk. The cost is more raw-material storage, handling and supplier management.
2. Operations: the biggest gain. One standard recipe and process at Agra gives the same taste in every outlet, in India and Germany. Quality is built in at source, and continuous improvement (kaizen) can be applied directly. It needs capacity planning: demand of 4,00,000 units against capacity of 5,00,000.
3. Outbound logistics: QBL must now pack and ship blends and frozen items to Division-D outlets and to Germany, with export documents and cold chain where needed. That is more work, but consolidated shipments give economies of scale and tighter control.
4. Marketing and sales: 'authentic, in-house NIWALA spice blends' becomes a USP. It supports the differentiation strategy and the food-safety and traceability claims that matter in Europe.
5. Service: consistent taste and fewer quality complaints bring more repeat visits and loyalty, and a complaint can be traced back to its batch quickly.
Overall: making the blends in-house adds cost and logistics work but strengthens quality control, consistency and the brand. It fits TQM and QBL's strategy of differentiation with cost leadership.
questions.trap: Writing about support activities (HR, technology, procurement). The question asks only for primary activities.

questions.subject: IDT
questions.chapter: Value of Supply (s.15 CGST + Rule 27 CGST Rules)
questions.topic: Consideration partly in kind: open market value
questions.ask: Find the value of TechFab's machine supply and the GST on it, and advise the accountant on the right valuation approach. (5 + 1 marks)
questions.clue: "QBL also provided 100 kilograms of specialized, high-grade spices... as consideration"
think: Consideration = money + spices, so price is not the sole consideration. The s.15 transaction value fails -> valuation rules.
Chapter clear -> IDT -> Value of Supply -> Rule 27 (consideration not wholly in money): open market value comes first.
OMV given = ₹8,85,000 including GST -> ₹7,50,000 excluding GST -> GST at 18% = ₹1,35,000.
Do not add the ₹40,000 of spices. That route (money + money value) applies only when OMV is not known.

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT: Value of Supply
index_keywords: section 15 transaction value price sole consideration
rule 27 consideration not wholly in money

questions.solve:
S.15: the transaction value applies only when the parties are unrelated and price is the sole consideration. Here QBL also gives spices, so price is not the sole consideration and Rule 27 applies.
Rule 27(a): value = open market value. OMV = full value in money excluding GST = 8,85,000 × 100/118 = ₹7,50,000.
GST at 18% = ₹1,35,000 (IGST, or CGST + SGST, depending on the place of supply).
Rule 27(b) (money + money value of the non-money consideration = 7,50,000 + 40,000 = 7,90,000) is used only when OMV is not available, which is not the case here.
Also: the 100 kg of spices QBL hands over is a separate supply by QBL to TechFab (barter), and QBL pays GST on it.
questions.answer:
Provision: under s.15, value is the transaction value only if supplier and recipient are unrelated and price is the sole consideration. Where consideration is not wholly in money, Rule 27 of the CGST Rules applies, in this order: (a) open market value; (b) if OMV is not available, money + the money value of the non-monetary consideration, if known at the time of supply; (c) the value of supplies of like kind and quality; (d) the cost-based or residual method.
Analysis: QBL paid money and also gave 100 kg of spices (₹40,000), so price is not the sole consideration. The transaction value cannot be used; Rule 27(a) applies.
(i) Value and GST
Open market value incl. GST: ₹8,85,000
Value excl. GST (8,85,000 × 100/118): ₹7,50,000
GST at 18%: ₹1,35,000
(ii) Advice to Mr Vivek: value the supply at its open market value of ₹7,50,000 under s.15 read with Rule 27(a). Do not add the ₹40,000 of spices; money + non-money value is used only when OMV is not known. Separately, the spices handed over are QBL's own supply to TechFab and attract GST in QBL's hands.
questions.icai: Same as ICAI: value ₹7,50,000; GST ₹1,35,000. The barter point on the spices is extra.
questions.trap: Adding the ₹40,000 to get ₹7,90,000. The OMV is given, so it governs.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.chapter: Professional Ethics (Code of Ethics; Second Schedule to the CA Act); SA 230 Audit Documentation
questions.topic: Confidentiality of client information; ownership of working papers
questions.ask: The banks ask CA. Lalit for extracts of his working papers on fixed assets. What are his duties on client confidentiality and disclosure to third-party lenders?
questions.clue: "formally requested CA. Lalit to provide detailed extracts from his audit working papers"
think: A third party wants the auditor's working papers -> confidentiality: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule + SA 200 / SA 230.
Chapter clear -> Audit SM -> Professional Ethics -> Clause (1) Part I Second Schedule. Working papers are the auditor's property.
Rule: no disclosure without the client's consent or a legal duty. Extracts are given only at the auditor's discretion; otherwise it is misconduct.

look_up.where: ICAI SM Audit: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors; SA 230

questions.solve: Under Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule, a CA in practice commits misconduct if he discloses information gained in an engagement to anyone other than the client, without the client's consent or a legal requirement. The duty continues after the engagement. Under SA 200, SA 230 and SQC 1, working papers belong to the auditor; he may at his discretion give extracts to the client, but others have no right to them. The banks are third parties, so CA. Lalit may share extracts only with QBL's written consent from a competent person (e.g., the Board or MD), and even then at his discretion. Otherwise he should refuse and suggest QBL gives the information itself.
questions.answer:
• Provision: under Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the CA Act, 1949, disclosing client information to a third party without the client's consent, or other than as required by law, is professional misconduct. The duty continues after the engagement ends.
• SA 200 and SA 230 / SQC 1: the auditor must keep information confidential, and audit working papers are the auditor's property. He may at his discretion give extracts to the client, but third parties have no right to them.
• Application: the nationalised bank and the consortium are third parties. CA. Lalit should not hand over working-paper extracts on fixed-asset valuation and useful life just because they ask.
• What he may do: obtain QBL's written consent from a competent authority (Board or MD). Then, at his discretion, share limited extracts, preferably with a disclaimer on reliance, or ask QBL to give the information to the banks directly.
• Conclusion: disclosing without the client's consent would make CA. Lalit guilty of professional misconduct.
questions.trap: Thinking a lender's request, or the bank's earlier loan, gives a right to the working papers. Only the client's consent or the law does.

questions.clue: "contributes over 25% of the consolidated revenue"; "19.5% of total expenses of previous accounting year"

Chapter clear -> Law -> SEBI LODR -> Reg 24(1) ID on the board of an unlisted material subsidiary (>20%); Reg 24(4) significant transactions (>10%); Reg 23(2) subsidiary RPT approval.

Test: (i) only Pluto's management reports, not ABC ✗; (ii) the threshold is 10%, so 19.5% must be reported ✗; (iii) an ID is needed only on material (>20%) unlisted subsidiaries, not all ✗; (iv) audit committee approval is needed, so it is true.

questions.solve:
(i) Under Reg 24(4), the management of the unlisted subsidiary (Pluto) regularly places a statement of all significant transactions before the listed entity's board. ABC, a group company, has no such duty, so 'both' is incorrect.

Write the six parameters, then link them to OTL (EUR/USD revenue against INR, the $10 million payable).

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM: Risk Management

questions.solve: The SM list is: government action, nominal interest rates (IRP), inflation (PPP), natural calamities, war/coup/rebellion and change of government. Then add the OTL-specific angle: currency mix of receivables and payables, and the timing of the $10 million payment.
questions.answer:
Currency risk depends on economic developments and on government action. Parameters OTL should track:
1. Government action: policy moves can shift a currency sharply (e.g., Brexit pushed the pound to multi-decade lows). Watch trade, tariff and capital-control decisions in the US, the EU and India.
2. Nominal interest rates: under interest rate parity, interest-rate differences drive forward rates and capital flows (US Fed/ECB vs RBI rates).
3. Inflation rates: under purchasing power parity, higher inflation weakens a currency over time.
4. Natural calamities: disasters disrupt the economy and weaken the currency.
5. War, coup or rebellion: political shocks cause sudden, large moves.
6. Change of government: a new government's stance on foreign investment and trade changes the currency outlook.
For OTL specifically: track the EUR/INR and USD/INR trend against its pricing, the mix of receivables by currency, and the $10 million payable due in 6 months. This tells it what to hedge (forwards/options) and whether to invoice in INR.
questions.icai: Same as ICAI (the six parameters). The OTL-specific lines are extra.
questions.trap: Writing hedging techniques (forwards, options) instead of the parameters that identify the risk.

questions.solve:
(i) The asset is non-monetary, so it stays at the transaction-date rate (₹88) and no exchange difference arises on it (ICDS VI). The EUR creditor is monetary; restating it at ₹92 adds ₹20 lakh to the liability (5,00,000 × 4). But for an asset acquired from outside India, s.43A governs (the Act overrides ICDS): the change in liability is added to actual cost only when payment is made. Payment is due in September 2026, so nothing is adjusted or deducted for FY 2024-25.
(ii) Actual cost = 5,00,000 × ₹88 = ₹4,40,00,000.
(iii) Put to use 15.10.2024, i.e., 168 days (less than 180), so half rates apply.
Normal: 4.40 crore × 15% × 50% = ₹33,00,000.
Additional u/s 32(1)(iia) (new P&M of a manufacturer): 4.40 crore × 20% × 50% = ₹44,00,000; the balance ₹44 lakh is allowed in FY 2025-26.
Total ₹77,00,000.
questions.answer:
(i) Treatment of the exchange difference on 31.03.2025
• ICDS VI: TECH M is a non-monetary item, carried at the transaction-date rate (₹88/EUR). No exchange difference arises on the asset.
• The EUR 5,00,000 creditor is monetary; at ₹92 it rises by ₹20,00,000. But it relates to an asset acquired from outside India, so s.43A applies (the Act prevails over ICDS): any increase or decrease in the liability is added to or deducted from actual cost only in the year the payment is made.
• Payment is due in September 2026, so there is no adjustment to cost and no deduction of the ₹20 lakh in FY 2024-25.

(ii) Actual cost on 31.03.2025 = EUR 5,00,000 × ₹88 = ₹4,40,00,000

(iii) Depreciation for FY 2024-25 (put to use 15.10.2024 = 168 days, i.e., less than 180 days)
Normal: ₹4,40,00,000 × 15% × 50% = ₹33,00,000
Additional u/s 32(1)(iia): ₹4,40,00,000 × 20% × 50% = ₹44,00,000 (assuming OTL has not opted for s.115BAA)
Total depreciation allowable = ₹77,00,000. The remaining additional depreciation of ₹44,00,000 is allowed in FY 2025-26.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI: no adjustment, cost ₹4.40 crore, ₹33 lakh + ₹44 lakh. ICAI neither totals these nor mentions the ₹20 lakh restatement of the liability.
questions.trap: Capitalising the ₹20 lakh at ₹92/EUR at year-end. s.43A works only on actual payment.
